replacement: Mihail Makarovitch was not at all efficient at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he had little education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he applied them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.

“I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He had never formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs. He simply picked them up from year to year, so to speak, and added to what he knew through practice, without ever meaning to. And he was a landowner himself, too. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would find some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors there that evening, but he didn’t know which ones. As it happened, the prosecutor was at that moment playing whist at the captain’s with Varvinsky, our district doctor. Varvinsky was a young man who had just come to us from Petersburg, where he had taken a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, was really only the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor. He was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to consumption, and married to a fat, childless wife. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good mind and even a kind heart. The trouble with him seemed to be only this: he thought himself abler than he was. That made him seem constantly ill at ease. He also had higher, even artistic, leanings, toward psychology for instance, toward a special study of the human heart and a special knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He felt wronged on this account. He believed he had been passed over in the service, and he was firmly convinced that in higher circles he was not properly valued and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to resign and take up criminal cases as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him deeply: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am running ahead.

But Marfa kept on screaming. She saw that her master’s window was open and a candle was alight in it, so she ran over and began calling Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she looked in at the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master lay on his back on the floor, not moving. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table brightly lit up the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed from the window and out of the garden. She drew the bolt of the big gate and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Mother and daughter were both asleep, but Marfa’s desperate, unceasing screams and her knocking at the shutter woke them. Shrieking and screaming incoherently, Marfa still managed to tell them the main fact and beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was spending the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way Marya Kondratyevna remembered that about eight o’clock she had heard a dreadful scream from the garden next door. That must have been Grigory’s scream of “Parricide!” uttered when he caught hold of Mitya’s leg.

I will say briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull smashed in. But with what? Most probably with the same weapon that had struck Grigory. And the moment that weapon was found, Grigory, who was at once given all possible medical help, told in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They searched with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. In the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay, there was no sign of disorder. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope. On it was written: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below that Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been taken. On the floor they also found a piece of narrow pink ribbon, which had been tied around the envelope.

But the inquiry, the search and the formalities in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house held them all up. It took time, and so they sent someone ahead to Mokroe two hours before they set out. This was the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had come into town the morning before to collect his pay. His orders were not to raise the alarm when he reached Mokroe. He was to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and to find witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told. He kept his identity secret and gave no one the slightest hint of his secret business, except his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and he noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch’s face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. Trifon Borissovitch had carried off the box with the pistols and put it in a suitable place. Only after four o’clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials arrive, the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer, in two carriages each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, to carry out a post-mortem on the body next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.
“I’m not guilty! I’m not guilty of that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him, yes. But I’m not guilty. Not I.”

“Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the one most to blame!” shouted the police captain, threatening her with his hand. But he was stopped at once, and firmly. The prosecutor simply grabbed him.
